one_liner: Schubfach-derived shortest double/float-to-string converter, about 2.4x faster than Ryu (the algorithm behind std::to_chars) on random doubles.
what_it_does: xjb prints IEEE-754 float and double values as the shortest decimal string that round-trips, producing the same digits as Schubfach. The library is one source file plus a header (src/ftoa.cpp, src/ftoa.h) exposing char* xjb_ftoa(double, char* buf) and a float overload; src/ftoa_json.cpp is a variant whose output satisfies RFC 8259 and ECMAScript number formatting. It is not a std::to_chars replacement: it has no [first,last) range, no error code, no precision or fixed/scientific modes, and its own text format.
how_it_is_fast: It is a reworked Schubfach: one 64x128-bit multiplication by a cached power of ten yields the candidate digits, and the shortest-digit and rounding decision is a handful of comparisons written to avoid mispredicted branches (README algorithm listing), instead of Ryu's digit-removal loop. Digit generation writes all 16-17 digits at once with SIMD (SSE2/SSSE3/SSE4.1, an AVX-512 IFMA/VBMI path credited to Daniel Lemire, a NEON path by Dougall Johnson), then fixes the decimal-point position with a shuffle or memmove. Exponent-dependent layout data comes from about 15-18 KB of tables built at compile time (a 368-byte compressed-table variant exists in bench/), so the hot path has few data-dependent branches.
when_to_use: JSON or CSV serializers that print many doubles (ssrJSON and jsoniter-scala use it): random full-range doubles measured 60.5 cycles vs 142.5 for Ryu and 105.8 for Dragonbox on a Zen 4 laptop with GCC 13.3.0.
Workloads dominated by long values (scientific data, 15-17 significant digits) or arbitrary bit patterns, where xjb's cost stays at about 56-64 cycles while Ryu takes 127-192.

x86-64 builds with SSE4.1 or AVX-512 IFMA, or AArch64/Apple Silicon with NEON; the README's April 2026 charts put xjb64 at about 43 cycles on the 7840H (icpx) and about 21 on M1 (derived from the SVG bar geometry).
Code that can take the output format as-is, or that wants the JSON-specific variant.
when_not_to_use: You need std::to_chars or printf semantics: precision, fixed or scientific modes, std::chars_format, error codes, or identical text (std::to_chars prints 1000 as '1000' and 1.2e23 as '1.2e+23'; xjb prints '1000.0' and '1.2e23').

Inputs are mostly short decimals or small integers: in the same GCC 13.3.0 run, dragonbox_full (45.8-67.9 cycles) and jnum beat xjb64 (about 75) for doubles in [0,1) with 1-11 significant digits, yyjson wins for 1-2 digit integers, and jnum wins for 9-17 digit integers, because xjb's cost is nearly constant regardless of digit count.
Big-endian targets (on the roadmap, not supported) or toolchains without C++20-era features; no MSVC result is published although MSVC intrinsic paths exist.
Projects needing settled licensing: the README says MIT while LICENSE and every source header say Apache-2.0 (open issue #25, 2026-10-06), and the README credits parts of the code to zmij.
Risk-averse code bases: a single-maintainer project with 46 stars whose src/ftoa.cpp had a one-byte buffer overrun fixed in July 2026 (PR #22); pin a commit at or after that fix.

integration.form: source-drop (src/ftoa.cpp + src/ftoa.h; src/ftoa_json.cpp for JSON output)
integration.dependencies: none (standard C headers; optional compiler intrinsics for SSE2/SSSE3/SSE4.1/AVX-512 IFMA+VBMI or NEON, picked from -march flags)
integration.min_toolchain: Not documented; the code uses C++20 features (designated initializers, [[unlikely]], constexpr-built tables) and the bench builds with -std=c++20 on GCC, Clang, Apple clang and icpx (icpx needs -no-ftz).
integration.platforms: x86-64 and AArch64 with SIMD paths, scalar fallback elsewhere; little-endian only
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; the function is stateless and reads only constant tables (derived from source), so concurrent calls are safe.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same shortest round-trip digits as Ryu/Schubfach, but a C-style char* API with its own output format ('1000.0', '1.2e23', '-nan', '-0.0') instead of std::to_chars's range, error code and standard formatting

gotchas: The output buffer must be at least 34 bytes for double and 21 for float even though the longest double string is 24 characters: the SIMD path stores whole 16-byte chunks. PR #22 raised the double requirement from 33 to 34 after a one-byte overrun for negative doubles with 16 integer digits, so callers sized to the old figure must update.

Harness details behind the cited numbers: the HTML result comes from the yybench harness in bench/util/benchmark.cpp, which at commit 933930c (the last commit touching the GCC 13.3.0 file) timed 100,000 values per dataset in a single pass (meansure_count = 1), through a function pointer, without -DNDEBUG. It is not the 16M-double loop in bench/main.cpp, which only prints to stdout, and not best-of-several runs. Single-pass noise shows in individual points: Ryu's [0,1) fixed-length curve jumps from 156.7 to 236.7 to 160.8 cycles at 3, 4 and 5 digits.

The benchmarked code is a separate copy (bench/xjb/float_to_string/ftoa.cpp at HEAD, bench/xjb/dtoa_xjb64_xjb32.cpp at 933930c), not src/ftoa.cpp, so fixes and tuning do not automatically flow between the shipped file and the measured one. In newer result files the xjb64_comp and yyjson rows are compile-time stubs that do no work.

src/ftoa.cpp also exports f16, f80, f128 and f256 overloads (taking raw bit patterns as integers) that ftoa.h does not declare and the README roadmap still lists f80/f128 as unsupported; treat them as experimental. Double verification in the harness checks round-trip and shortest length, but float verification is marked 'To be completed' (the README says 'make check' in bench/ confirms output identical to Schubfach).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick xjb over Dragonbox, Ryu or {fmt} when bulk shortest-format output dominates and you control the text format: in the author's harness it is 1.75x faster than Dragonbox's full-table build and 2.2x faster than fmt 12.1.0 on random doubles. Pick Dragonbox, {fmt} or Boost.Charconv when you need std-compatible formatting, a mature multi-maintainer library or mostly short decimals; fast_float and fast_double_parser cover the parsing direction.
verified_claims_summary: In the author's yybench run (GCC 13.3.0 -O3 -march=native, AMD Ryzen 7 7840H at about 5.1 GHz, Linux), converting full-range random doubles took 60.5 cycles each for xjb64 vs 142.5 for ulfjack's Ryu d2s, 105.8 for Dragonbox and 132.2 for fmt 12.1.0, about 2.4x faster than Ryu; on Apple M1 with Apple clang 17 it was 31.4 vs 98.7 (3.1x). std::to_chars itself was not timed: Ryu stands in for the algorithm that libstdc++, libc++ and MSVC STL use, and Ryu writes a different exponent format.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-08-10, v1.5.0 charts from April 2026) but a single-maintainer project; Apache-2.0 per LICENSE and source headers despite the README's MIT line, so vendor src/ftoa.cpp and ftoa.h at a pinned commit after the PR #22 buffer fix.
